title: 7 Presentation Habits for Experts Who Build the Slides First
author: Said Well
summary: This Said Well essay argues that most experts prepare a talk backwards, opening PowerPoint first so that the deck becomes the plan, when a deck only organises the speaker's material and not the audience's experience of it. The author, who says he has coached over 300 speakers, starts with two sentences written before any slide exists: where the audience is at the start, and what will have changed in them by the end. He explains that rooms remember the opening and the close best, so those two moments deserve word-for-word preparation while the middle is only outlined. He shares a story about over-preparing a talk until his mind ran a sentence ahead of his mouth, and concludes that a full script or a loose outline can both work but half-memorising fails. The seven habits cover finding out who is in the room, the two-sentence move, scripting the opening and close, using stories, outlining rather than scripting, finishing early, and building slides last. The piece ends with a pitch for a paid guide bundle, which the summary ignores.
points: The core move is a two-sentence brief, written before opening the deck, that names where the audience starts and what must have changed in them by the end; anything that does not serve that gap comes out.

Because listeners retain the beginning and end best, the first three and last three sentences should be scripted and rehearsed while the middle is only outlined, and writing the close before the middle makes the middle easier to write.

The author's over-preparation story shows that a half-memorised script leaves a speaker fluent enough to recite but not present enough to respond to the room, so a speaker should either commit to a full script or to an outline.
Overrunning loses the audience before the content fails, so planning for forty minutes in a fifty-minute slot protects the close and earns goodwill.
Slides are a document rather than the talk, so they should be built last and kept only where they show something the voice cannot, such as a trend or a genuinely visual comparison.
quotes: I have coached over 300 speakers and run more than 30 events, and this is the most common structural error I see. The deck becomes the plan, and a deck is a poor plan, because it organises your material rather than the audience’s experience of it.
A room does not want a survey. They came with something specific they need, which may be two of your nine sections, and the other seven are costing you their attention while you deliver them.
Your opening buys the attention you spend in the middle. Nothing after it gets a fair hearing if those first sentences were spent on your name, your job title, and how pleased you are to be here.
Sentence two: where are they at the end? Not what you will have covered. What will have changed in them.
That gap is the entire talk. Anything that does not serve the move comes out, however good it is, and most of what you were planning to include does not serve it.
The rule is not that scripting fails, it is that half-memorising fails, because you end up fluent enough to recite and not fluent enough to be present.
Nobody has ever complained about a presentation that ended early, and finishing with ten minutes spare gives the room something they value more than your last three slides.
A slide earns its place by showing something your voice cannot. A trend, a photograph, a comparison that is genuinely visual.
